titleBlock.headline: Organ-Specific Proteomic Aging Clocks Predict Disease and Longevity Across Diverse Populations
titleBlock.authors: Wang, Y., Xiao, S., Liu, B. et al.

researchSummary:
This is a summary of the scientific study.
Not affiliated with the study authors or their institutions.
whatIsClock: An organ-specific aging clock quantifies the biological age of an individual organ using organ-enriched proteins circulating in blood plasma (annotated via GTEx tissue expression with >=4-fold organ enrichment). Unlike chronological age, the 'organ age gap' reflects whether a specific organ is biologically older or younger than same-aged peers.

Pairwise correlations between organ age gaps within the same person are weak (mean r = 0.16 in UKB), proving that human organs age asynchronously. Relying solely on a whole-body clock obscures critical organ-specific vulnerabilities.

Researchers profiled 2,916 plasma proteins (Olink Explore 3072) to train LightGBM models for 1 organismal clock (240 proteins) and 10 organ-specific clocks across 48,393 participants in the UK Biobank (n = 43,616), China Kadoorie Biobank (n = 3,977), and US Nurses' Health Study (n = 800).

studyOverview.label: Objective
studyOverview.value: Develop and externally validate 10 organ-specific and 1 organismal proteomic aging clocks to predict incident chronic diseases, multimorbidity, and mortality.

studyOverview.label: Design
studyOverview.value: LightGBM + Boruta feature selection on 2,916 Olink plasma proteins (418 organ-enriched via GTEx).

studyOverview.label: Participants
studyOverview.value: n = 48,393 total: UK Biobank (n = 43,616), China CKB (n = 3,977), and US NHS (n = 800).

studyOverview.label: Assessments
studyOverview.value: Plasma proteomics, brain MRI structure, GWAS (29,629 participants), lifestyle factors, and 11–30 yr disease/mortality follow-up.

scorecardOverview.title: The Question
scorecardOverview.content: Can a single blood draw resolve the independent biological aging rates of 10 distinct human organ systems—and do organ-specific clocks outperform whole-body clocks across diverse global populations?

scorecardOverview.title: The Methodology
scorecardOverview.content: Using Olink Explore 3072 plasma proteomics (2,916 proteins) and GTEx tissue mapping, the authors trained LightGBM clocks in the UK Biobank (n = 43,616) and externally validated them in China (CKB, n = 3,977) and the USA (NHS, n = 800), achieving cross-cohort r = 0.98 and 0.93.

scorecardOverview.title: The Breakthrough
scorecardOverview.content: Organ age gaps are weakly correlated (mean r = 0.16) and strongly predict organ-matched and systemic diseases. Having 5+ extremely aged organs raises mortality risk 7.8-fold, whereas 5+ super-youthful organs cuts mortality by 60% and dementia risk by 75%.

keyFindings.title: Predictive Power
keyFindings.desc: Organ-specific age gaps significantly predicted 121 of 187 organ-disease pairs (65% after FDR correction), outperforming whole-body organismal clocks and established clinical risk scores.

keyFindings.title: Brain Aging & APOE4 Resilience
keyFindings.desc: The brain aging clock had the strongest link to all-cause mortality (HR = 1.44 per 1-SD) and stratified Alzheimer's risk across APOE haplotypes—with a super-youthful brain conferring resilience even in APOE4 carriers.

keyFindings.title: Cross-Ancestry Robustness
keyFindings.desc: Validated across UK (n = 43,616), Chinese (n = 3,977), and US (n = 800) cohorts with cross-cohort correlation r = 0.93–0.98, plus parsimonious 5–20 protein panels for clinical translation.

keyFindings.title: Genetic & Lifestyle Modifiability
keyFindings.desc: GWAS mapped brain aging to 38 SNPs (including GABBR1 and ECM1), while healthy sleep, physical activity, oily fish, and non-smoking significantly decelerated brain, intestine, and pancreas aging.

organProfiles.name: Brain Clock
organProfiles.proteins: 117 enriched proteins (e.g., APOD, GFAP, NEFL, BCAN)
secondaryMetrics: 1.44x All-Cause Mortality Risk (strongest of all organs, q = 3.35e-74)
1.89x Progression from MCI to Dementia (q = 3.23e-8)
1.52x Multiple Sclerosis Risk & 1.30x Parkinson's Disease Risk
Independent predictor of 14 out of 17 neuropsychiatric & physical outcomes
organProfiles.mechanism: Links synaptic loss, glial activation, and GABBR1/ECM1 genetic pathways to cortical atrophy and cognitive decline; super-youthful brain ageotype buffers APOE4 genetic risk.

organProfiles.name: Kidney Clock
secondaryMetrics: 1.78x Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) Risk (q = 3.31e-78)
2.08x Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) Risk (q = 5.93e-152)
Explains 38% of multi-organ association with T2D and 17% with CKD
Strongly linked to hypertension, BUN, and creatinine elevation
organProfiles.mechanism: Captures early glomerular and tubular proteostasis decline years prior to clinical eGFR drop, acting as a central hub for cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity.

organProfiles.name: Intestine Clock
secondaryMetrics: 1.93x Chronic Kidney Disease Risk (q = 1.45e-98)
1.54x Type 2 Diabetes Risk (q = 4.47e-65)
Top driver of combined physical + neuropsychiatric multimorbidity
Significantly decelerated by healthy dietary habits (vegetables, oily fish)
organProfiles.mechanism: Reflects intestinal barrier integrity and gut-organ axis signaling; accelerated intestinal aging drives systemic endotoxemia, renal inflammation, and insulin resistance.

organProfiles.name: Artery Clock
secondaryMetrics: Second strongest correlation with systemic organismal aging (despite only 4% protein overlap)
Independently predicts incident dementia and cognitive decline alongside the Brain clock
Replicated associations with myocardial infarction and hypertension in UKB, CKB, and NHS
organProfiles.mechanism: Tracks arterial stiffening, endothelial dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier breakdown, bridging cardiovascular pathology and neurodegenerative white-matter injury.

organProfiles.name: Heart Clock
secondaryMetrics: Strongly predicts incident heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial infarction
Independently associated with cognitive decline and incident dementia
Cross-organ link to chronic liver and renal disease progression
organProfiles.mechanism: Quantifies myocardial remodeling, natriuretic stress, and microvascular perfusion deficits with as few as 5 age-related proteins.

organProfiles.name: Immune System Clock
organProfiles.proteins: 109 enriched proteins (76 age-related proteins in final clock)
secondaryMetrics: Second largest organ-enriched proteome pool (109 GTEx-enriched proteins)
Predicts all-cause mortality, severe infections, and multi-organ chronic disease
Correlates with systemic C-reactive protein (CRP) and shorter leukocyte telomeres
organProfiles.mechanism: Measures thymic involution, myeloid skewing, and chronic sterile inflammation that accelerate aging across peripheral solid organs.

findingsCallout: Individuals with super-youthful brain ageotypes showed lower dementia risk, suggesting possible resilience even in genetically higher-risk APOE4 groups.
keyTakeaway: Measuring the biological age of individual organs via blood proteins accurately predicts disease onset, progression, and mortality across diverse global populations—proving that multi-organ extreme aging compounds mortality 7.8-fold while super-youthful organs confer profound protection.
protocolRecommendations: Monitor organ-specific biological age (via emerging proteomic panels) rather than relying solely on whole-body clocks to identify your fastest-aging 'weakest link' organ.
Target preventative protocols to accelerated organ systems (e.g., vascular & blood-pressure optimization for an aging artery/heart clock; sleep, exercise, and omega-3s for an aging brain clock).

Protect multiple organ systems simultaneously through modifiable lifestyle habits (non-smoking, restorative sleep, regular physical activity, and whole-food/oily-fish nutrition), which significantly decelerated brain, pancreas, and intestinal clocks.

mortalityLineChart.title: Mortality Risk by Extremely Aged Organs (> +1.5 SD)

messages: Participants with 5+ extremely aged organs face a 7.8-fold higher all-cause mortality risk.

dementiaLineChart.title: Dementia Risk by Extremely Aged Organs (> +1.5 SD)

messages: Having 5+ extremely aged organs increases incident dementia risk by 4.1-fold.

youthfulMortalityLineChart.title: Mortality Protection by Super-Youthful Organs (< -1.5 SD)

messages: Participants with 5+ super-youthful organs experience a 60% reduction in all-cause mortality (HR = 0.40).

youthfulDementiaLineChart.title: Dementia Protection by Super-Youthful Organs (< -1.5 SD)

messages: Having 5+ super-youthful organs reduces incident dementia risk by 75% (HR = 0.25).

conclusions: Organ-specific proteomic aging clocks provide a high-resolution, noninvasive map of biological aging across 10 major human organ systems.

Brain aging showed the strongest independent association with all-cause mortality (HR = 1.44) and neurodegenerative disease (dementia HR = 1.88), while super-youthful brain ageotypes buffered genetic APOE4 risk.

Multi-organ extreme aging compounds disease and mortality risk exponentially (up to 7.8x mortality risk for 5+ aged organs), whereas maintaining super-youthful organs cuts mortality by 60% and dementia risk by 75%.

structuredConclusions.title: Asynchronous Organ Aging Is the Norm
structuredConclusions.content: Pairwise correlations among the 10 organ age gaps are weak (mean r = 0.16 in UKB, 0.19 in CKB, 0.10 in NHS), proving that a single whole-body biological age score masks organ-specific disease trajectories.

structuredConclusions.title: Brain & Vascular Clocks Govern Survival
structuredConclusions.content: Brain aging independently predicted 14 of 17 health outcomes and exhibited the strongest mortality association (HR = 1.44 per 1-SD), while super-youthful brain proteomes conferred resilience against APOE4-driven Alzheimer's risk.

structuredConclusions.title: Dose-Dependent Risk vs. Youthful Resilience
structuredConclusions.content: Accumulating 1–2, 3–4, or 5+ extremely aged organs raises mortality risk 1.7x, 3.8x, and 7.8x; conversely, having 1–2, 3–4, or 5+ super-youthful organs lowers mortality by 25%, 40%, and 60% and dementia by 19%, 49%, and 75%.
